sections.title: Schematic symbols
sections.summary: The symbol for every part the lessons use

blocks.text: How the lessons draw each part, and what to look for when you meet it in someone else's schematic. In the figures each wire takes the colour of its voltage; here everything is in ink.

A line is a wire, and all of one line is at one voltage. Lines that meet at a T are joined. Many schematics also put a dot on every join, and draw lines that cross without a dot as not touching: when in doubt, look for the dot.

items.name: Battery or supply
items.means: Two plates: the long one is +, the short one −. A battery of several cells is often drawn as several pairs; a bench supply is drawn the same way, with its voltage written beside it.

items.name: Resistor
items.means: A zigzag. European schematics draw a plain rectangle instead. The value is written beside it, often with the multiplier as the decimal point: 4k7 is 4.7 kΩ.

items.name: Lamp
items.means: A circle with a cross in it: a filament bulb. Its resistance rises as the filament heats, so it is not a fixed resistor.

items.name: Switch
items.means: A lever hinged at one contact, drawn open. Closed, it is a wire. Tap one in a figure to flip it.

items.name: Ground
items.means: The 0 V every other voltage is measured from. Every ground symbol in a drawing is joined to every other, so the return wires can be left out.

items.name: Potentiometer
items.means: A resistor with an arrow touching it partway along: a divider whose tap, the wiper, slides. Three legs, the two ends of the track and the wiper.

items.name: Current source
items.means: A circle with an arrow: it pushes a set current the way the arrow points, whatever voltage that takes. More a way of thinking about a part than a part you buy.

items.name: Fuse
items.means: A box with the wire running through it. It is a wire until too much current for too long melts it open.

items.name: Steady-power load
items.means: This workbook's box for a load that takes the same watts whatever its voltage, such as a pump, a converter or an inverter. Real schematics draw the part itself or a labelled box.

items.name: Signal source
items.means: A circle with a wave in it: a voltage that keeps changing, such as a signal generator or a guitar pickup. A square in the circle means a square wave.

items.name: Op-amp
items.means: A triangle pointing the way the signal goes, with a − and a + input and one output. Its power pins are often left off the drawing, but it still needs them.

items.name: Capacitor
items.means: Two plates with a gap between. An electrolytic, which has a + and a − leg, is drawn with one plate curved or a + by it; fit it the right way round.

items.name: Inductor or coil
items.means: A row of humps: a coil of wire. A relay's coil is one, which is why it kicks back when it is switched off.

items.name: Diode
items.means: An arrow into a bar. Current flows the way the arrow points, from anode to cathode; the bar is the cathode, the end with the stripe on the part.

items.name: LED
items.means: A diode with two arrows coming off it, the light. It drops about 2 V (red) to 3 V (blue) and needs a resistor to set its current.

items.name: NPN transistor
items.means: Base on the left, collector at the top, emitter at the bottom with its arrow pointing out. A small current into the base lets a bigger one flow from collector to emitter. A PNP's arrow points in.

items.name: N-channel MOSFET
items.means: Gate on the left, not touching the channel: that gap is the insulation that means the gate draws no steady current. A voltage on the gate turns it on from drain (top) to source (bottom).

sections.title: Wire and trace sizes
sections.summary: Resistance and current by cable size, voltage drop over a run, and fusing

blocks.text: Drop = current × resistance of the whole loop, out and back. Aim for 3% or less on power runs. Fuse below the cable's rating, above the load's current, as close to the battery as you can.

Ratings depend on insulation, bundling and air temperature; take the cable maker's figure over this table. Trace widths on a board follow the same rule: a 1 oz copper trace 0.25 mm wide carries well under an amp.

blocks.text: Biasing a common-emitter stage on a single supply: choose the current, put about a tenth of the supply across Re, size Rc to drop about half the supply, and set R1 and R2 so the base sits a diode’s drop above the emitter, with R2’s current several times the base current.

sections.title: Using a multimeter
sections.summary: Volts across, amps through, and what each reading tells you

blocks.text: Volts are measured **across**: one probe on each side of the part, circuit left alone. Amps are measured **through**: break the loop and put the meter in the gap.

items: Volts: dial to V (DC is the straight-line symbol), black lead in COM, red in V.
Touch black to ground or one side of the part, red to the other. A minus sign means red is lower than black.
Amps: dial to A or mA, black in COM, red moved to the A or mA socket.
Break the loop (lift a wire, open a link) and put the probes in the gap, so the current goes through the meter.
Move the red lead back to V when you're done. A meter left in amps and put across a battery shorts it and blows its fuse.

blocks.caption: Volts across, amps through. Tap a wire to place a probe or cut the loop.
